sourceClaims: Hypervigilance at the level of outcomes.

Hypervigilance at the level of outcomes. The foundation of the Type A pattern. Not a personality trait, a fear response that has been running so long it looks like a management style. The fear underneath: something will go wrong, someone will get hurt, or the situation will fall apart if I release my grip. Self-control registers as 10. Anything less registers as loss. The delta between perceived control and actual control is the zone of active saboteur behavior. Anger layers in as a do-as-I-say mechanism, authority used to close the control gap quickly. Entitlement provides the justification: it is not just that I need to control this. It is that I am right to. Competition drives the adversarial edge, not just winning but not-losing, which is a different frequency entirely.
The moment control begins to slip. Uncertainty in outcomes. Others not performing to expectation. Delegation without confirmation. Silence where confirmation should be.

The future feels uncertain. Something may happen, but you cannot quite predict what. That uncertainty can produce anxiety before anything has actually gone wrong. The grip tightens in an attempt to make the outcome predictable: you check, correct, and take over. For a moment, control can feel like safety and the anxiety may ease. Then the room gets smaller: less space for the people around you to move, less room in you to trust without checking first. This is one possible pattern, not an explanation for every act of control. Reflection: When you cannot predict the outcome, what do you feel you need to take control of?
